newsitem.title: USA: FDA panel backs Bristol-Myers Kaposi drug.
newsitem.headline: FDA panel backs Bristol-Myers Kaposi drug.

text.p: A U.S. Food and Drug Administration advisory panel on Monday voted unanimously to approve Bristol-Myers Squibb's paclitaxel (Taxol) as a second-line therapy for Kaposi's sarcoma, a cancer affecting 20,000 AIDS patients.
The firm was seeking accelerated approval of Taxol, based on early safety and efficacy data and demonstration of superiority over existing therapies.
The drug is already approved in the United States as a second-line therapy for metastatic breast and ovarian cancer.

Eight of the panelists voted for full approval -- meaning that the company could market the drug without doing confirmatory studies. But four panelists said they only supported accelerated approval, saying that they worried that once the drug is available without restrictions, that little more will be discovered about its toxicity.
The FDA is not bound by the panel's advice, but generally follows it.
In addition to presenting impressive response rates, BMS showed the panel photographs of patients whose Kaposi's lesions -- black and usually raised -- had disappeared or faded significantly.
"I've never seen such dramatic improvement," said Donald Abrams of San Francisco General Hospital, who reviewed the BMS data for the committee.
However, there were reported problems with Taxol's safety profile. It causes suppression of the bone marrow and of white blood cells, known as neutropenia.
In the two BMS phase two clinical trials, a majority of patients developed serious neutropenia, which led to opportunistic infections in 84 percent of patients.
In the first BMS study, conducted at the National Cancer Institute (NCI), 20 of 29 patients enrolled responded to treatment, with the median response lasting seven months.
In the second study, 59 percent of patients taking a lower dose responded, with one having a complete remission, and 32 having a partial remission. The response lasted a median of 10 months.
In both trials, patients were extremely sick, with most having CD4 counts lower than 200 cells per cubic millimeter.
The FDA did not significantly differ with BMS's reponse figures.

There are few second-line therapies for Kaposi's sarcoma. Many patients benefit from first-line treatment with either a combination of chemotherapy drugs, or more recently, liposomal forms of anthracyclines. But, according to AIDS advocates, those drugs generally only have a three-to-four month window of efficacy.

A consortium of seven AIDS advocacy groups, including AIDS Project Los Angeles, Gay Men's Health Crisis, and Treatment Action Group, urged approval of Taxol, but suggested that it only be used in conjunction with granulocyte-colony stimulating factor. G-CSF, made by Amgen Inc, helps boost white blood cell counts.

Taxol was first approved in the United States in 1992, and has since been approved in 65 nations, for metastatic ovarian cancer. The drug has also been approved by FDA and 37 other countries as a second-line therapy for breast cancer.
